claim: CskAS BMDMs express normal levels of myeloid and macrophage surface markers F4/80, CD11b, and CD11c.
source: We generated bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) from CskAS mice and verified that they express normal levels of myeloid and macrophage surface markers (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1 demonstrating expression of F4/80, CD11b, and CD11c surface markers.

claim: Within three seconds of adding 3-IB-PP1 to CskAS BMDMs, there is a 60–80% loss of phosphorylation of the SFK inhibitory-tail tyrosine.
source: Within three seconds of adding 3-IB-PP1 to CskAS BMDMs, we observed a 60–80% loss of phosphorylation of the SFK inhibitory-tail tyrosine and a 100–400% increase in activation-loop tyrosine phosphorylation (Figure 2, left lanes).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2 showing decreased pLynY507 (inhibitory-tail phosphorylation) within seconds of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.

claim: Within three seconds of adding 3-IB-PP1 to CskAS BMDMs, there is a 100–400% increase in activation-loop tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Within three seconds of adding 3-IB-PP1 to CskAS BMDMs, we observed a 60–80% loss of phosphorylation of the SFK inhibitory-tail tyrosine and a 100–400% increase in activation-loop tyrosine phosphorylation (Figure 2, left lanes).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2 showing increased pSFKY416 (activation-loop phosphorylation) within seconds of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.

claim: Activated SFKs reach a maximum fivefold to eightfold above basal levels within 90 seconds of 3-IB-PP1 addition.
source: Activated SFKs continued to accumulate, reaching a maximum fivefold to eightfold above basal within 90 s.
evidence: Inferred from the time course data in Figure 2 showing progressive accumulation of activated SFKs.

claim: 3-IB-PP1 treatment has no effect on SFK phosphorylation in WT BMDMs.
source: As expected from the low affinity of 3-IB-PP1 for WT Csk (Tan et al., 2014), 3-IB-PP1 treatment had no effect on SFK phosphorylation in WT BMDMs (Figure 2, right lanes).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2 showing no change in SFK phosphorylation in WT cells treated with 3-IB-PP1, and by citation to previous work demonstrating low affinity of 3-IB-PP1 for WT Csk.

claim: Zymosan depleted of TLR2 agonists (zymosandep) induces phosphorylation of the MAPK Erk in macrophages.
source: As expected, treatment with zymosandep induced phosphorylation of the MAPK Erk as well as phosphorylation of Akt (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3 showing pErk phosphorylation after zymosandep treatment.

claim: Zymosan depleted of TLR2 agonists (zymosandep) induces phosphorylation of Akt in macrophages.
source: As expected, treatment with zymosandep induced phosphorylation of the MAPK Erk as well as phosphorylation of Akt (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3 showing pAkt phosphorylation after zymosandep treatment.

claim: Downstream signaling in response to zymosandep is dependent on Syk activation.
source: Abrogation of downstream signaling in the presence of the Syk inhibitor BAY 61-3606 (Figure 3A) and the SFK inhibitor PP2 (Figure 3B) confirmed the dependence of zymosandep signaling on SFK and Syk activation, especially within the first 5 min of signaling before Syk begins to be activated independently of the SFKs (Takata et al., 1994; Fitzer-Attas et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3A showing loss of Erk and Akt phosphorylation when BAY 61-3606 is added, and by citations to previous work on Syk-independent activation.

claim: Downstream signaling in response to zymosandep is dependent on SFK activation, especially within the first 5 minutes.
source: Abrogation of downstream signaling in the presence of the Syk inhibitor BAY 61-3606 (Figure 3A) and the SFK inhibitor PP2 (Figure 3B) confirmed the dependence of zymosandep signaling on SFK and Syk activation, especially within the first 5 min of signaling before Syk begins to be activated independently of the SFKs (Takata et al., 1994; Fitzer-Attas et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3B showing loss of Erk and Akt phosphorylation when PP2 is added, and by citations to previous work on Syk-independent activation.

claim: Syk begins to be activated independently of the SFKs after the first 5 minutes of signaling.
source: Abrogation of downstream signaling in the presence of the Syk inhibitor BAY 61-3606 (Figure 3A) and the SFK inhibitor PP2 (Figure 3B) confirmed the dependence of zymosandep signaling on SFK and Syk activation, especially within the first 5 min of signaling before Syk begins to be activated independently of the SFKs (Takata et al., 1994; Fitzer-Attas et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work demonstrating SFK-independent Syk activation.

claim: SFK activation by 3-IB-PP1 fails to induce significant levels of Erk phosphorylation.
source: In contrast to zymosandep, SFK activation by 3-IB-PP1 failed to induce significant levels of Erk phosphorylation (Figure 4A, arrow).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4A showing minimal Erk phosphorylation after 3-IB-PP1 treatment compared to zymosandep.

claim: Small changes in Erk phosphorylation in response to 3-IB-PP1 treatment are equivalent to the effect of pulse-spinning cells without additional stimulation.
source: Small changes in Erk phosphorylation were occasionally seen in response to 3-IB-PP1 treatment. However, within each experiment, any minimal increase in Erk phosphorylation with 3-IB-PP1-treatment was equivalent to the effect of pulse-spinning the cells without any additional stimulation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4B comparing Erk phosphorylation with and without 3-IB-PP1 after pulse-spinning.

claim: SFKs, Syk, and PLCγ2 are phosphorylated robustly in response to 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Interestingly, upstream activators, including the SFKs, Syk, and PLCγ2, were phosphorylated robustly in response to 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4A showing phosphorylation of pSFKY416, pSykY352, and pPLCγ2Y1217 after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.

claim: SFK activation by 3-IB-PP1 produces more robust membrane-proximal signaling than zymosandep.
source: In fact, SFK activation by this maximally effective dose of 3-IB-PP1 (Tan et al., 2014) produced much more robust membrane-proximal signaling than did zymosandep, where an increase in SFK activation-loop phosphorylation was not even detectable.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of immunoblot intensities in Figure 4A and supported by citation to previous work on 3-IB-PP1 dosing.

claim: An increase in SFK activation-loop phosphorylation is not detectable in response to zymosandep.
source: In fact, SFK activation by this maximally effective dose of 3-IB-PP1 (Tan et al., 2014) produced much more robust membrane-proximal signaling than did zymosandep, where an increase in SFK activation-loop phosphorylation was not even detectable.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4A showing no visible increase in pSFKY416 after zymosandep treatment.

claim: 3-IB-PP1 does not suppress Erk phosphorylation in WT BMDMs treated with zymosandep.
source: To minimize the possibility that an off-target effect of 3-IB-PP1 blocks Erk phosphorylation by a CskAS-independent mechanism, we treated WT BMDMs with a combination of zymosandep and increasing concentrations of 3-IB-PP1 and found no suppression of Erk phosphorylation (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4C showing maintained Erk phosphorylation in WT cells treated with zymosandep plus 3-IB-PP1.

claim: M-CSF-induced Erk and Akt signaling is unaffected by 3-IB-PP1 in WT BMDMs.
source: Signaling in response to the growth factor M-CSF, which initiates Erk and Akt signaling through the CSF-1 receptor tyrosine kinase pathway (Pixley and Stanley, 2004), was similarly unaffected by 3-IB-PP1 in WT BMDMs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing no change in M-CSF-induced Erk and Akt phosphorylation with 3-IB-PP1 in WT cells, and by citation to previous work on M-CSF signaling.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation in WT BMDMs is insensitive to 3-IB-PP1.
source: We also tested 3-IB-PP1 specificity by treating WT and CskAS BMDMs with 3-IB-PP1 and assessing global tyrosine phosphorylation by immunoblotting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). As expected, tyrosine phosphorylation in WT BMDMs was insensitive to 3-IB-PP1.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing no change in global tyrosine phosphorylation in WT cells treated with 3-IB-PP1.

claim: The specific inhibitory effect of 3-IB-PP1 on CskAS, not a nonspecific effect, causes the measured signaling responses.
source: We conclude that the specific inhibitory effect of 3-IB-PP1 on CskAS, not a nonspecific effect, causes the measured signaling responses.
evidence: Inferred from multiple specificity control experiments showing no off-target effects in WT cells.

claim: 3-IB-PP1 impairs Erk and Akt responses to M-CSF in CskAS BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, we found that 3-IB-PP1 impaired Erk and Akt responses to M-CSF in CskAS BMDMs, suggesting that the failure of Erk signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1 arises from an active signaling blockade rather than a quantitative failure of membrane-proximal signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing reduced M-CSF-induced Erk and Akt phosphorylation when 3-IB-PP1 is added to CskAS cells.

claim: The failure of Erk signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1 arises from an active signaling blockade rather than a quantitative failure of membrane-proximal signaling.
source: Interestingly, we found that 3-IB-PP1 impaired Erk and Akt responses to M-CSF in CskAS BMDMs, suggesting that the failure of Erk signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1 arises from an active signaling blockade rather than a quantitative failure of membrane-proximal signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 3-IB-PP1 suppresses M-CSF signaling in CskAS cells despite robust membrane-proximal signaling.

claim: Actin remodeling agents do not restore Erk phosphorylation in response to 3-IB-PP1 in BMDMs.
source: We performed analogous experiments with BMDMs by adding Cytochalasin D, Latrunculin A, or Jasplakinolide in combination with 3-IB-PP1 or zymosandep (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). Although actin remodeling affected Erk phosphorylation in response to zymosandep, it did not increase Erk phosphorylation in response to 3-IB-PP1.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 showing no increase in Erk phosphorylation when actin-remodeling agents are combined with 3-IB-PP1.

claim: The signaling blockade between activated SFKs and Erk in the absence of receptor clustering is fundamentally different in macrophages than in thymocytes.
source: This finding suggests that the signaling blockade between activated SFKs and Erk in the absence of receptor clustering is fundamentally different in macrophages than in thymocytes, reflecting the different functions of actin remodeling and costimulatory pathways in signal initiation.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of actin remodeling on 3-IB-PP1-induced signaling in macrophages versus thymocytes.

claim: Priming with IFN-γ enables 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through Erk in CskAS BMDMs.
source: Strikingly, priming with IFN-γ enabled 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through Erk (Figure 5A, arrow) as well as Akt, the MAPK JNK, and the calcium-sensitive transcription factor NFAT (Figure 5B, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5A and 5B showing robust Erk, Akt, JNK, and NFAT activation after 3-IB-PP1 treatment in IFN-γ-primed cells.

claim: Priming with IFN-γ enables 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through Akt in CskAS BMDMs.
source: Strikingly, priming with IFN-γ enabled 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through Erk (Figure 5A, arrow) as well as Akt, the MAPK JNK, and the calcium-sensitive transcription factor NFAT (Figure 5B, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B showing robust Akt phosphorylation after 3-IB-PP1 treatment in IFN-γ-primed cells.

claim: Priming with IFN-γ enables 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through JNK in CskAS BMDMs.
source: Strikingly, priming with IFN-γ enabled 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through Erk (Figure 5A, arrow) as well as Akt, the MAPK JNK, and the calcium-sensitive transcription factor NFAT (Figure 5B, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B showing robust JNK phosphorylation after 3-IB-PP1 treatment in IFN-γ-primed cells.

claim: Priming with IFN-γ enables 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through NFAT in CskAS BMDMs.
source: Strikingly, priming with IFN-γ enabled 3-IB-PP1 treatment to stimulate robust downstream signaling through Erk (Figure 5A, arrow) as well as Akt, the MAPK JNK, and the calcium-sensitive transcription factor NFAT (Figure 5B, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B showing NFAT1 activation (faster migration) after 3-IB-PP1 treatment in IFN-γ-primed cells.

claim: Priming with IFN-γ has a comparatively small effect on downstream signaling in response to zymosandep.
source: Priming with IFN-γ had a comparatively small effect on downstream signaling in response to zymosandep.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of immunoblot intensities in Figure 5A showing similar Erk phosphorylation in primed and unprimed cells treated with zymosandep.

claim: Priming BMDMs with IFN-γ generally increases membrane-proximal signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: Priming BMDMs with IFN-γ generally increased membrane-proximal signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1. We observed more robust phosphorylation of DAP12, Syk, LAT, PLCγ1, PLCγ2, Cbl, PI3K, HS1, Vav, and Fak in primed cells than in unprimed cells (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing increased phosphorylation of multiple membrane-proximal signaling proteins in primed cells.

claim: Phosphorylation of signaling proteins downstream of Syk is more sustained in primed cells treated with 3-IB-PP1.
source: In addition to being more robust, phosphorylation of signaling proteins downstream of Syk (e.g., LAT, PLCγ1/2, c-Cbl, and PI3K) was more sustained in primed cells (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5 showing prolonged phosphorylation of LAT, PLCγ1/2, c-Cbl, and PI3K in primed cells over time.

claim: Syk phosphorylation continues to increase over time during treatment with 3-IB-PP1 in either primed or unprimed cells.
source: This observation is especially striking because Syk phosphorylation continued to increase over time during treatment with 3-IB-PP1 in either primed or unprimed cells and also during treatment with zymosandep and was therefore kinetically uncoupled from downstream signaling through Erk and Akt.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5 showing progressive increase in pSykY352 over time in both primed and unprimed cells.

claim: Syk phosphorylation is kinetically uncoupled from downstream signaling through Erk and Akt.
source: This observation is especially striking because Syk phosphorylation continued to increase over time during treatment with 3-IB-PP1 in either primed or unprimed cells and also during treatment with zymosandep and was therefore kinetically uncoupled from downstream signaling through Erk and Akt.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Syk phosphorylation increases continuously while Erk/Akt phosphorylation does not follow the same pattern.

claim: Priming enhances the phosphorylation of negative regulatory proteins Sirpα, SHIP1, and SHP-1 in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: Surprisingly, we found that priming actually enhanced the phosphorylation of proteins that negatively regulate signaling, including the ITIM-containing protein Sirpα, the inositol phosphatase SHIP1, and the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 (Figure 6), which led to activation of the negative-regulatory adaptor Dok-3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6 showing increased phosphorylation of Sirpα, SHIP1, and SHP-1 in primed cells treated with 3-IB-PP1.

claim: Priming leads to activation of the negative-regulatory adaptor Dok-3 in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: Surprisingly, we found that priming actually enhanced the phosphorylation of proteins that negatively regulate signaling, including the ITIM-containing protein Sirpα, the inositol phosphatase SHIP1, and the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 (Figure 6), which led to activation of the negative-regulatory adaptor Dok-3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing Dok-3 association with SHIP1 and Dok-3 tyrosine phosphorylation.

claim: Priming does not generally inhibit negative feedback in macrophages.
source: These data indicate that priming does not generally inhibit negative feedback in macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that negative regulatory proteins are actually more phosphorylated in primed cells.

claim: The SFK Lyn is the primary kinase responsible for phosphorylating and activating ITIMs and their associated phosphatases.
source: However, the increased phosphorylation of negative regulatory proteins in primed cells provided a clue to the upstream factor driving signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1: Since the SFK Lyn is the primary kinase responsible for phosphorylating and activating ITIMs and their associated phosphatases (Ravetch and Lanier, 2000; Lowell, 2010), we hypothesized that Lyn is driving signaling and that its expression or function is enhanced by IFN-γ priming.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on Lyn's role in ITIM phosphorylation.

claim: 3-IB-PP1 fails to induce robust Erk phosphorylation in cells treated with IFN-γ for 4 hours or less.
source: We found that 3-IB-PP1 failed to induce robust Erk phosphorylation in cells treated with IFN-γ for 4 hr or less (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7A showing minimal Erk phosphorylation in cells primed for 0.5, 2, or 4 hours.

claim: IFN-γ priming for 6 or 8 hours produces modest Erk phosphorylation in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: IFN-γ priming for 6 hr or 8 hr produced modest Erk phosphorylation, and priming for 16 hr led to robust Erk phosphorylation in response to 3-IB-PP1.
evidence: Inferred from the time course data in Figure 7A showing intermediate Erk phosphorylation at 6-8 hours.

claim: IFN-γ priming for 16 hours leads to robust Erk phosphorylation in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: IFN-γ priming for 6 hr or 8 hr produced modest Erk phosphorylation, and priming for 16 hr led to robust Erk phosphorylation in response to 3-IB-PP1.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7A showing strong Erk phosphorylation after 16 hours of priming.

claim: A priming-dependent transcriptional change potentiates Erk signaling after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: This temporal pattern strongly suggests that a priming-dependent transcriptional change potentiates Erk signaling after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the time course showing that priming effects require several hours to develop, consistent with transcriptional regulation.

claim: Lyn expression is substantially increased by IFN-γ priming.
source: Blotting for total Lyn protein in the presence and absence of IFN-γ revealed that Lyn expression was substantially increased by priming (Figure 7A, left lanes, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and that Lyn expression correlated with the ability of 3-IB-PP1 to induce Erk signaling (Figure 7A, right lanes).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7A showing increased total LynA protein in IFN-γ-primed cells.

claim: Lyn expression correlates with the ability of 3-IB-PP1 to induce Erk signaling.
source: Blotting for total Lyn protein in the presence and absence of IFN-γ revealed that Lyn expression was substantially increased by priming (Figure 7A, left lanes, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and that Lyn expression correlated with the ability of 3-IB-PP1 to induce Erk signaling (Figure 7A, right lanes).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7A showing parallel increases in LynA expression and Erk phosphorylation across different priming durations.

claim: GM-CSF priming produces an intermediate degree of Lyn upregulation that corresponds with an intermediate level of Erk phosphorylation after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: We also tested an alternative priming agent, the growth factor GM-CSF (Goodridge et al., 2009), and found an intermediate degree of Lyn upregulation that corresponded with an intermediate level of Erk phosphorylation after 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7B showing intermediate LynA expression and Erk phosphorylation in GM-CSF-primed cells, and by citation to previous work on GM-CSF priming.

claim: Among the SFKs and other membrane-proximal signaling proteins examined, only Lyn and Csk are upregulated in both GM-CSF-primed and IFN-γ-primed BMDMs.
source: Moreover, among the SFKs and other membrane-proximal signaling proteins examined, only Lyn and Csk itself were upregulated in both GM-CSF-primed and IFN-γ-primed BMDMs (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7C showing selective upregulation of Lyn and Csk in both priming conditions.

claim: Lyn deficiency renders IFN-γ-primed BMDMs completely unresponsive to 3-IB-PP1 in terms of Erk signaling.
source: Strikingly, Lyn deficiency rendered BMDMs completely unresponsive to the signal-potentiating effects of priming; Lyn−/−CskAS BMDMs primed with IFN-γ failed to signal through Erk after 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 8A, arrow) even though they express normal macrophage surfaces markers (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8A showing no Erk phosphorylation in Lyn−/−CskAS cells treated with 3-IB-PP1, and by flow cytometry data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing normal surface markers.

claim: The magnitude of downstream signaling in response to zymosandep is unaffected by Lyn deficiency.
source: In contrast, the magnitude of downstream signaling in response to zymosandep was unaffected by Lyn deficiency.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8A showing similar Erk phosphorylation in CskAS and Lyn−/−CskAS cells treated with zymosandep.

claim: Hck and Fgr cannot compensate for the loss of Lyn to promote downstream signaling during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: This reveals a fundamental difference in the requirement for Lyn in the SFK-mediated signaling initiated by 3-IB-PP1 compared to receptor clustering. Hck and Fgr, the other major SFKs expressed in macrophages, cannot compensate for the loss of Lyn to promote downstream signaling during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Lyn−/−CskAS cells fail to signal through Erk after 3-IB-PP1 treatment despite expressing Hck and Fgr.

claim: In ligand-induced receptor clustering, Hck and Fgr compensate for Lyn and downstream signaling is able to proceed.
source: However, in ligand-induced receptor clustering Hck and Fgr do compensate for Lyn and downstream signaling is able to proceed.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Lyn−/−CskAS cells show normal Erk phosphorylation in response to zymosandep.

claim: In Lyn−/−CskAS BMDMs treated with 3-IB-PP1, Hck and Fgr induce phosphorylation of Vav, Syk, LAT, PLCγ, and SHIP1.
source: When we treated Lyn−/−CskAS BMDMs with 3-IB-PP1, the remaining SFKs, Hck and Fgr, induced the phosphorylation of Vav, Syk, LAT, PLCγ, and SHIP1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8A showing phosphorylation of these proteins in Lyn−/−CskAS cells treated with 3-IB-PP1.

claim: Phosphorylation of membrane-proximal signaling proteins in Lyn−/−CskAS BMDMs treated with 3-IB-PP1 is less robust than in CskAS BMDMs but still surpasses the level detected after zymosandep treatment.
source: Although phosphorylation of these membrane-proximal signaling proteins was less robust in Lyn−/−CskAS BMDMs, the level of proximal signaling still surpassed the level detected after zymosandep treatment.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of immunoblot intensities in Figure 8A.

claim: Lyn activity is specifically required for priming-enabled Erk signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: We conclude that Lyn activity is specifically required for priming-enabled Erk signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Lyn-deficient cells fail to signal through Erk after 3-IB-PP1 treatment despite priming.

claim: Hck and Fgr expression levels are not affected by Lyn expression in BMDMs.
source: No changes in expression of the other major macrophage SFKs, Hck and Fgr, were observed in Lyn-deficient B cells (Chan et al., 1997), but we nevertheless tested Hck and Fgr expression in WT and Lyn−/− BMDMs. As expected, Hck and Fgr expression levels were not affected by Lyn expression (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8B showing similar Hck and Fgr levels in WT and Lyn−/− cells, and by citation to previous work in B cells.

claim: Hck is upregulated in both WT and Lyn−/− BMDMs in response to IFN-γ priming.
source: Hck is, however, upregulated in both WT and Lyn−/− BMDMs in response to IFN-γ priming (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8B showing increased Hck expression in IFN-γ-primed cells of both genotypes.

claim: Hck is unlikely to be the dominant factor promoting signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: Because it is not upregulated during GM-CSF priming and fails to rescue signaling in Lyn−/− cells, Hck is unlikely to be the dominant factor promoting signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Hck upregulation does not correlate with signaling rescue and is not seen with GM-CSF priming.

claim: Lyn−/− cells are not generally impaired in their response to IFN-γ.
source: However, the normal upregulation of Hck in response to IFN-γ indicates that Lyn−/− cells are not generally impaired in their response to IFN-γ.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Hck is upregulated normally in Lyn−/− cells in response to IFN-γ.

claim: Some Lyn-specific function is responsible for downstream signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1 in IFN-γ primed cells.
source: This supports our conclusion that some Lyn-specific function is responsible for downstream signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1 in IFN-γ primed cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Lyn deficiency specifically blocks 3-IB-PP1-induced signaling despite normal IFN-γ responses.

claim: The amount of Lyn protein decreases during the course of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Interestingly, we found that the amount of Lyn protein decreased during the course of 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 8A, double arrow), and this led us to quantify the levels of all of the SFKs during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8A showing decreased total LynA over time during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.

claim: LynA is preferentially depleted during 3-IB-PP1 treatment of CskAS BMDMs.
source: We examined the levels of Lyn, Hck, and Fgr protein during 3-IB-PP1-treatment of CskAS BMDMs and found that LynA was preferentially depleted (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 9A showing selective loss of LynA compared to other SFKs.

claim: Total LynA levels in unprimed cells treated with 3-IB-PP1 decrease by 60% within 2 minutes.
source: Total LynA levels in unprimed cells treated with 3-IB-PP1 decreased by 60% within 2 min, whereas Hck, LynB, and Fgr each decreased by only about 30% during the same time frame (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 9B showing quantified loss of LynA protein.

claim: Hck, LynB, and Fgr each decrease by only about 30% within 2 minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Total LynA levels in unprimed cells treated with 3-IB-PP1 decreased by 60% within 2 min, whereas Hck, LynB, and Fgr each decreased by only about 30% during the same time frame (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 9B showing quantified loss of other SFK proteins.

claim: The E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl is robustly phosphorylated after treating CskAS cells with 3-IB-PP1.
source: After treating CskAS cells with 3-IB-PP1, the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl was robustly phosphorylated (Figure 5B), leading us to speculate that activated Lyn might be ubiquitinated as part of a c-Cbl-mediated negative feedback loop (Rao et al., 2002; Kyo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B showing p-c-CblY700 phosphorylation, and by citations to previous work on c-Cbl-mediated ubiquitination.

claim: LynA immunoprecipitates are more polyubiquitinated after treatment with 3-IB-PP1.
source: We used immunoprecipitation to isolate LynA and Hck in the presence or absence of 3-IB-PP1 and assessed the degree of ubiquitination of each immunoprecipitate by immunoblotting. We found that LynA immunoprecipitates were indeed more polyubiquitinated after treatment with 3-IB-PP1 (Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data in Figure 9C showing increased ubiquitin signal in LynA immunoprecipitates after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.

claim: LynA itself is modified by ubiquitination after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: To confirm that LynA itself was modified by ubiquitination, we also used immunoblotting to show laddering of LynA and activation-loop-phosphorylated SFKs in whole-cell lysates (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 9—figure supplement 2 showing laddering pattern characteristic of ubiquitination.

claim: Hck does not show laddering characteristic of ubiquitination after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: To confirm that LynA itself was modified by ubiquitination, we also used immunoblotting to show laddering of LynA and activation-loop-phosphorylated SFKs in whole-cell lysates (Figure 9—figure supplement 2). Such laddering was not seen with Hck.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 9—figure supplement 2 showing no laddering in Hck blots.

claim: LynA differs from LynB only in a 21 amino-acid insert in its unique region.
source: LynA differs from LynB only in a 21 amino-acid insert in its unique region, and this unique insert contains a predicted ubiquitination site (K40) and a phosphorylation site (Y32) (Figure 9—figure supplement 3) (Stanley et al., 1991; Yi et al., 1991; Radivojac et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Figure 9—figure supplement 3 and citations to previous work on LynA/LynB structure and post-translational modification predictions.

claim: The unique insert in LynA contains a predicted ubiquitination site (K40) and a phosphorylation site (Y32).
source: LynA differs from LynB only in a 21 amino-acid insert in its unique region, and this unique insert contains a predicted ubiquitination site (K40) and a phosphorylation site (Y32) (Figure 9—figure supplement 3) (Stanley et al., 1991; Yi et al., 1991; Radivojac et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Figure 9—figure supplement 3 and citations to previous work on post-translational modification predictions.

claim: The unique insert in LynA regulates LynA uniquely and marks LynA preferentially for ubiquitination and degradation.
source: We therefore speculate that this insert regulates LynA uniquely and marks LynA preferentially for ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural differences between LynA and LynB and the observed differential degradation.

claim: Both Lyn and Hck lose inhibitory-tail phosphorylation during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Although both Lyn and Hck lost inhibitory-tail phosphorylation during 3-IB-PP1 treatment, the inhibitory tail of Lyn was dephosphorylated preferentially (5% Lyn vs 24% Hck tail phosphorylation remaining after 1 min) (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 10B showing loss of pLynY507 and pHckY527.

claim: The inhibitory tail of Lyn is dephosphorylated preferentially compared to Hck (5% Lyn vs 24% Hck tail phosphorylation remaining after 1 minute).
source: Although both Lyn and Hck lost inhibitory-tail phosphorylation during 3-IB-PP1 treatment, the inhibitory tail of Lyn was dephosphorylated preferentially (5% Lyn vs 24% Hck tail phosphorylation remaining after 1 min) (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 10B showing quantified differences in inhibitory-tail dephosphorylation.

claim: Both Lyn isoforms are activation-loop phosphorylated more rapidly than Hck and Fgr.
source: Similarly, we found that both Lyn isoforms were activation-loop phosphorylated more rapidly than Hck and Fgr.
evidence: Inferred from the time course data in Figure 10C showing earlier peak activation of LynA and LynB.

claim: LynA and LynB reach maximum activation-loop phosphorylation within 3–6 seconds of 3-IB-PP1 addition.
source: LynA and LynB reached maximum activation-loop phosphorylation within 3–6 s of 3-IB-PP1 addition, whereas activated Hck and Fgr continued to accumulate for the first 1–3 min (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 10C showing time course of activation-loop phosphorylation.

claim: Activated Hck and Fgr continue to accumulate for the first 1–3 minutes after 3-IB-PP1 addition.
source: LynA and LynB reached maximum activation-loop phosphorylation within 3–6 s of 3-IB-PP1 addition, whereas activated Hck and Fgr continued to accumulate for the first 1–3 min (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 10C showing time course of activation-loop phosphorylation.

claim: The active form of LynA is short-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: The active form of LynA was short-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 10C), mirroring the pattern of total protein degradation.
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 10C showing rapid decline in activated LynA.

claim: Only 20% of activation-loop-phosphorylated LynA remains after 3 minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Only 20% of the activation-loop-phosphorylated LynA remained after 3 min, but the other activated SFKs, LynB, Hck, and Fgr persisted at 70%, 80%, and 90%, respectively, of the maximum level.
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 10C showing quantified loss of activated LynA.

claim: Activated LynB, Hck, and Fgr persist at 70%, 80%, and 90%, respectively, of the maximum level after 3 minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Only 20% of the activation-loop-phosphorylated LynA remained after 3 min, but the other activated SFKs, LynB, Hck, and Fgr persisted at 70%, 80%, and 90%, respectively, of the maximum level.
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 10C showing quantified persistence of other activated SFKs.

claim: Activated LynA is uniquely transient during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: All the SFKs were activated relative to their basal levels (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), but activated LynA was uniquely transient during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 10—figure supplement 2 showing fold-increase in activation and rapid decline of LynA.

claim: LynA protein is subject to degradation in IFN-γ-primed cells during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: LynA protein was also subject to degradation in IFN-γ-primed cells during 3-IB-PP1 treatment, but due to its increased basal expression LynA protein persisted at significant levels through the 3- to 5-min time frame of Erk activation (Figure 11A, Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 11A showing LynA degradation over time in primed cells.

claim: Due to increased basal expression, LynA protein persists at significant levels through the 3- to 5-minute time frame of Erk activation in IFN-γ-primed cells.
source: LynA protein was also subject to degradation in IFN-γ-primed cells during 3-IB-PP1 treatment, but due to its increased basal expression LynA protein persisted at significant levels through the 3- to 5-min time frame of Erk activation (Figure 11A, Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 11A showing sustained LynA levels in primed cells during the critical signaling window.

claim: At each time point during the first 5 minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment, LynA levels are threefold higher in primed cells than in unprimed cells.
source: At each time point during the first 5 min of 3-IB-PP1 treatment, LynA levels were threefold higher in primed cells than in unprimed cells (Figure 11B).
evidence: Supported by densitometry data in Figure 11B showing quantified comparison of LynA levels in primed versus unprimed cells.

claim: The greater abundance of LynA protein in primed cells serves as a buffer against degradation, allowing LynA activity to be sustained above a threshold level and enabling Erk signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1.
source: We conclude that the greater abundance of LynA protein in primed cells serves as a buffer against degradation, allowing LynA activity to be sustained above a threshold level and enabling Erk signaling in response to 3-IB-PP1.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between sustained LynA levels and Erk phosphorylation in primed cells.

claim: Macrophages are myeloid-derived hematopoietic cells that guard against infection and orchestrate a broad immune response to pathogens.
source: Macrophages are myeloid-derived hematopoietic cells that guard against infection and orchestrate a broad immune response to pathogens.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about macrophage function.

claim: Macrophages survey tissues for signs of pathogen invasion and present antigen to T cells.
source: Bridging the innate and adaptive immune systems, they survey tissues for signs of pathogen invasion and present antigen to T cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about macrophage function.

claim: When activated, macrophages engulf and destroy foreign organisms and secrete cytokines.
source: When activated, they engulf and destroy foreign organisms and secrete cytokines (Mosser and Edwards, 2008; Murray and Wynn, 2011; Wynn et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on macrophage activation.

claim: Inappropriate activation of macrophages can cause tissue injury.
source: While macrophage activity promotes an effective immune response to tissue distress, inappropriate activation of macrophages can cause tissue injury.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about macrophage pathology.

claim: Accumulation of activated macrophages is linked to diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and obesity.
source: Accumulation of activated macrophages is linked to diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and obesity (Murray and Wynn, 2011; Wynn et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on macrophage-associated diseases.

claim: Macrophage stimulation through ITAM- and hemi-ITAM-coupled receptors initiates pathogen destruction via phagocytosis and the production of reactive oxygen species.
source: Macrophage stimulation through immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM)- and hemi-ITAM-coupled receptors initiates pathogen destruction via phagocytosis and the production of reactive oxygen species, which require activated macrophages to be physically close to the pathogen.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ITAM receptor signaling.

claim: Large-diameter stimuli that are more likely to be associated with pathogenic particles nucleate large-scale receptor clusters, forming a phagocytic synapse.
source: One mechanism by which cells make this distinction is by using receptor clustering to sense the size of a potential stimulus. Large-diameter stimuli that are more likely to be associated with pathogenic particles nucleate large-scale receptor clusters, forming a signaling complex called a phagocytic synapse.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about receptor clustering and phagocytic synapse formation.

claim: Small-diameter stimuli induce only small-scale or transient receptor clusters.
source: In contrast, small-diameter stimuli induce only small-scale or transient receptor clusters (Goodridge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on receptor clustering.

claim: In mast cells, treatment with a high dose of weak stimulus can produce robust receptor phosphorylation without stable receptor clustering.
source: In mast cells, a related myeloid subtype, treatment with a high dose of weak stimulus can produce robust receptor phosphorylation without stable receptor clustering.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mast cell signaling.

claim: The membrane-proximal signaling patterns produced by weak stimuli in mast cells are qualitatively different than those produced in response to a strong stimulus.
source: Interestingly, the resulting membrane-proximal signaling patterns, as well as the associated immunopathologies, are qualitatively different than those produced in response to a strong stimulus (Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014), which indicates that myeloid cells can distinguish between strong and weak stimuli beyond simply sensing the degree of receptor phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on mast cell signaling patterns.

claim: Myeloid cells can distinguish between strong and weak stimuli beyond simply sensing the degree of receptor phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, the resulting membrane-proximal signaling patterns, as well as the associated immunopathologies, are qualitatively different than those produced in response to a strong stimulus (Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014), which indicates that myeloid cells can distinguish between strong and weak stimuli beyond simply sensing the degree of receptor phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that signaling patterns differ qualitatively between strong and weak stimuli.

claim: Receptor engagement initiates interactions with an active pool of Src-family tyrosine kinases (SFKs).
source: Receptor engagement initiates interactions with an active pool of Src-family tyrosine kinases (SFKs), which phosphorylate intracellular ITAMs within the receptor, the tyrosine kinase Syk, cytoskeleton-associated proteins, and other membrane-proximal signaling proteins (Lowell, 2010; Goodridge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on SFK signaling.

claim: SFKs phosphorylate intracellular ITAMs within the receptor, the tyrosine kinase Syk, cytoskeleton-associated proteins, and other membrane-proximal signaling proteins.
source: Receptor engagement initiates interactions with an active pool of Src-family tyrosine kinases (SFKs), which phosphorylate intracellular ITAMs within the receptor, the tyrosine kinase Syk, cytoskeleton-associated proteins, and other membrane-proximal signaling proteins (Lowell, 2010; Goodridge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on SFK substrates.

claim: Membrane-proximal signaling initiates downstream signaling, including the PLCγ-MAPK and PI3K-Akt pathways.
source: This membrane-proximal signaling initiates downstream signaling, including the phospholipase Cγ-mitogen-activated protein kinase (PLCγ-MAPK) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B/Akt (PI3K-Akt) pathways.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about signaling pathways.

claim: The signaling cascades initiated by the SFKs in response to strong stimuli enact a transcriptional program of macrophage activation leading to microbicidal activity.
source: The signaling cascades initiated by the SFKs in response to strong stimuli then enact a transcriptional program of macrophage activation leading to microbicidal activity (Lowell, 2010; Byeon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on macrophage activation.

claim: Inflammatory cytokines secreted by other immune cells trigger inflammatory priming, a transcriptional program that increases macrophage reactivity.
source: For example, inflammatory cytokines secreted by other immune cells trigger a process termed inflammatory priming, a transcriptional program that increases macrophage reactivity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about inflammatory priming.

claim: Priming upregulates the expression of proteins involved in signal detection, pathogen killing, and stimulation of other immune cells.
source: Priming is known to upregulate the expression of proteins involved in signal detection, pathogen killing, and stimulation of other immune cells (Platanias, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on priming effects.

claim: Clustered receptors are immobilized within the cell membrane, participate in costimulatory interactions, and organize the signaling complex spatially.
source: Clustered receptors are immobilized within the cell membrane, participate in costimulatory interactions, and organize the signaling complex spatially, integrating SFK-dependent and SFK-independent steps into a productive signaling response (Sohn et al., 2008; Bethani et al., 2010; Dustin and Groves, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on receptor clustering.

claim: Csk phosphorylates the inhibitory-tail tyrosine of the SFKs, promoting an autoinhibited state.
source: Csk phosphorylates the inhibitory-tail tyrosine of the SFKs, promoting an autoinhibited state in which the SH2 domain of the SFK interacts with the phosphorylated inhibitory tail and constrains the kinase domain in an inactive conformation (Brown and Cooper, 1996; Okada, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on Csk function.

claim: The phosphatases CD45 and CD148 dephosphorylate the inhibitory-tail tyrosine of the SFK, releasing autoinhibition and enabling subsequent activation-loop autophosphorylation and full activation.
source: The phosphatases CD45 and CD148 dephosphorylate the inhibitory-tail tyrosine of the SFK, releasing this autoinhibition and enabling subsequent activation-loop autophosphorylation and full activation (Chow and Veillette, 1995; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on CD45 and CD148 function.

claim: The continuous competition of Csk and CD45/CD148 sets the steady state of SFK inhibitory-tail phosphorylation in the cell.
source: The continuous competition of Csk and CD45/CD148 sets the steady state of SFK inhibitory-tail phosphorylation in the cell.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SFK regulation.

claim: Inhibiting Csk activity disrupts the steady state of SFK inhibitory-tail phosphorylation, allowing CD45 and CD148 to initiate bulk SFK activation unopposed.
source: Inhibiting Csk activity disrupts this steady state, allowing CD45 and CD148 initiate bulk SFK activation unopposed (Schoenborn et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on Csk inhibition.

claim: 3-IB-PP1 is 30-fold more selective for CskAS than for WT Csk.
source: The bulky structure of 3-IB-PP1 should increase its specificity for CskAS over WT kinases, and we have shown experimentally that 3-IB-PP1 is 30-fold more selective for CskAS than for WT Csk (Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work demonstrating selectivity.

claim: Macrophages express a distinct subset of Src family members (Lyn, Hck, and Fgr).
source: Macrophages express a distinct subset of Src family members (Lyn, Hck, and Fgr) (Lowell, 2004), and, unlike naive T cells, macrophages express the ITAM-proximal kinase Syk (Wang et al., 2010) and SFK-dependent negative-regulatory phosphatases associated with immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Veillette et al., 2002; Lowell, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on macrophage SFK expression.

claim: Unlike naive T cells, macrophages express the ITAM-proximal kinase Syk.
source: Macrophages express a distinct subset of Src family members (Lyn, Hck, and Fgr) (Lowell, 2004), and, unlike naive T cells, macrophages express the ITAM-proximal kinase Syk (Wang et al., 2010) and SFK-dependent negative-regulatory phosphatases associated with immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Veillette et al., 2002; Lowell, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on Syk expression.

claim: Macrophages express SFK-dependent negative-regulatory phosphatases associated with ITIMs.
source: Macrophages express a distinct subset of Src family members (Lyn, Hck, and Fgr) (Lowell, 2004), and, unlike naive T cells, macrophages express the ITAM-proximal kinase Syk (Wang et al., 2010) and SFK-dependent negative-regulatory phosphatases associated with immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Veillette et al., 2002; Lowell, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on ITIM-associated phosphatases.

claim: The responsiveness of macrophages to weak stimuli is regulated by a signaling checkpoint in which degradation of LynA occurs when weak or low-valency ligands engage surface receptors.
source: We propose that the responsiveness of macrophages to weak stimuli is regulated by a signaling checkpoint in which degradation of LynA occurs when weak or low-valency ligands engage surface receptors; by contrast, LynA expression is maintained but not required when strong or high-valency ligands induce large-scale receptor clustering.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: LynA expression is maintained but not required when strong or high-valency ligands induce large-scale receptor clustering.
source: We propose that the responsiveness of macrophages to weak stimuli is regulated by a signaling checkpoint in which degradation of LynA occurs when weak or low-valency ligands engage surface receptors; by contrast, LynA expression is maintained but not required when strong or high-valency ligands induce large-scale receptor clustering.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Signaling induced in the absence of significant receptor clustering is blocked at the level of Erk, JNK, Akt, and NFAT.
source: As a result, signaling induced in the absence of significant receptor clustering is blocked at the level of Erk, JNK, Akt, and NFAT, while signaling induced by high-valency receptor clustering proceeds through these pathways.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Signaling induced by high-valency receptor clustering proceeds through Erk, JNK, Akt, and NFAT pathways.
source: As a result, signaling induced in the absence of significant receptor clustering is blocked at the level of Erk, JNK, Akt, and NFAT, while signaling induced by high-valency receptor clustering proceeds through these pathways.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: When cells are primed with IFN-γ, they upregulate expression of LynA sufficiently that even weak or low-valency ligands can produce downstream Erk, JNK, Akt, and NFAT signaling.
source: However, when cells are primed with IFN-γ, they upregulate expression of LynA sufficiently that even weak or low-valency ligands can produce downstream Erk, JNK, Akt, and NFAT signaling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Priming sensitizes macrophages to small amounts of high-valency pathogen ligands.
source: While priming sensitizes macrophages to small amounts of high-valency pathogen ligands, it will also increase the chance to signaling to host-derived or nonpathogenic low-valency ligands that may lead to immunopathology.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the implications of priming.

claim: Priming increases the chance of signaling to host-derived or nonpathogenic low-valency ligands that may lead to immunopathology.
source: While priming sensitizes macrophages to small amounts of high-valency pathogen ligands, it will also increase the chance to signaling to host-derived or nonpathogenic low-valency ligands that may lead to immunopathology.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the implications of priming.

claim: When mast cells derived from Lyn−/− mice are reconstituted with LynA, LynA expression leads to more robust PLCγ phosphorylation and better association of PLCγ with the adaptor protein LAT in response to FcϵRI ligation.
source: However, such Lyn-deficient cells lack both LynA and LynB. When mast cells derived from Lyn−/− mice are reconstituted either with LynA or LynB, LynA expression leads to more robust PLCγ phosphorylation and better association of PLCγ with the adaptor protein LAT in response to FcϵRI ligation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from previous work on LynA function in mast cells.

claim: LynB expression drives the formation of a LynB-SHIP1 complex and impairs calcium and degranulation responses in mast cells.
source: In contrast, LynB expression drives the formation of a LynB-SHIP1 complex and impairs calcium and degranulation responses (Alvarez-Errico et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on LynB function in mast cells.

claim: A complex of Dok-3, SHIP1, and Grb2 associates with Slp76, Btk, and PLCγ and negatively regulates PLCγ, Ras/MAPK, and Akt function in B cells.
source: Studies in B cells have shown that a complex of Dok-3, SHIP1, and Grb2 associates with Slp76, Btk, and PLCγ and negatively regulates PLCγ, Ras/MAPK, and Akt function (Honma et al., 2006; Stork et al., 2007; Losing et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on Dok-3 function in B cells.

claim: Two phosphorylation sites of Dok-3 (Y378 and Y399) are not required for SHIP1-binding or inhibitory function.
source: Two phosphorylation sites of Dok-3 (Y378 and Y399) are not required for SHIP1-binding or inhibitory function (Lemay et al., 2000; Robson et al., 2004), and we speculate that these sites could sense LynA activity and block Dok-3 function.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on Dok-3 phosphorylation sites.

claim: Lyn ubiquitination in mast cells has been observed within 15–30 seconds of FcϵRI activation.
source: In fact, Lyn ubiquitination in mast cells has been observed within 15–30 s of FcϵRI activation (Kyo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on Lyn ubiquitination in mast cells.

claim: The LynA checkpoint would render macrophages refractory to restimulation by another weak stimulus, at least until redistribution at the membrane or new synthesis replenishes local reserves of LynA.
source: The LynA checkpoint would not only shut signaling down but also render macrophages refractory to restimulation by another weak stimulus, at least until redistribution at the membrane or new synthesis replenishes local reserves of LynA.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the implications of LynA degradation.

claim: Loss of negative-regulatory receptor tyrosine kinases Tyro3, Axl, and Mer exacerbates lupus-like disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease through enhanced Toll-like receptor signaling.
source: For example, loss of negative-regulatory receptor tyrosine kinases Tyro3, Axl, and Mer exacerbates lupus-like disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease through enhanced Toll-like receptor signaling (Rothlin et al., 2007; Lemke and Rothlin, 2008; Rothlin and Lemke, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on Tyro3, Axl, and Mer function.

claim: Loss of either SHP-1 or SHIP1 causes severe myeloproliferation, skin abscesses, and lung failure.
source: Loss of either SHP-1 or SHIP1, both negative regulators of ITAM signaling, causes severe myeloproliferation, skin abscesses, and lung failure (Van Zant and Shultz, 1989; Shultz et al., 1993; Tsui et al., 1993; Helgason et al., 1998; Abram et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on SHP-1 and SHIP1 deficiency.

claim: The LynA checkpoint constitutes a system by which macrophages sense inflammation and set basal sensitivity accordingly.
source: The LynA checkpoint constitutes an additional system by which macrophages sense inflammation and set basal sensitivity accordingly.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.
